8001:
Here's the last thing I found on YouTube -- Two Boxes at Once - 1979 (Bally Arcade).  It's an animation made by Mark McKernin.  It's unclear to me what the exact connection to the Bally Arcade is.  Was it actually made on a prototype ZGRASS, or developed for the UV-1 with the intention of giving the add-under this capability?  The animation itself strikes me as fairly simple.  I've seen BASIC graphics programs that strike me as similar.  Here's what the description says:

(1979) This is an example of early computer graphics animation on the Datamax UV-1, developed by students at the Electronic Visualization Lab. This animation was created by Mark McKernin.

More information can be found on the EVL website --
http://www.evl.uic.edu/core.php?mod=4&type=5&indi=133
and http://www.evl.uic.edu/core.php?mod=4&type=1&indi=336

The second link has a description by Tom DeFanti:

"The Datamax UV-1 was a pioneering computer designed by a working group of computer graphics artists at the University of Illinois at Chicago. The group, then known as the Circle Graphics Habitat, fostered an environment for the creation of experimental computer graphics, video production, and educational materials development. Over time the group became what is now the current EVL lab.

The basis for the Datamax UV-1 was the GRASS programing language, originally developed by Tom DeFanti for his 1974 Ohio State University Ph.D. thesis.

In 1977 DeFanti was introduced to Jeff Frederiksen, a chip designer working at Dave Nutting Associates. Nutting had been contracted by Midway, the videogame division of Bally, to create a standardized graphics driver chip. They intended to use it in most of their future arcade games, as well as a video game console they were working on which would later turn into the Astrocade. Midway was quite interested in seeing the GRASS language running on their system, and contracted DeFanti to port it to the platform.

The goal was to create a GRASS machine that could be marketed at a personal computer price point, a project that became known as the Z-Box. The version of the GRASS language running on the machine was GRASS3, which would become known as Zgrass. The work would never be released by Midway, but the Circle would produce machines based on it as the Datamax UV-1.

The project eventually evolved into a machine intended to to generate high-quality color graphics for output to videotape, and later as a titling system for use by cable television companies. In this capacity, it represents the first dedicated graphics workstation."

8013:
If it was first, I would give it much more slack, but besides the Magnavox
Odyssey in 1972 and Atari's home Pong in 1975, the Fairchild VES was
available in 1976, and got it about as right for a first try at a true
programmable game system as you can get. The fact that the Studio II came in
1977, is black and white, when even color home Pong systems were known
quantities by then, and that it only had keypads on the unit for controls,
when again a variety of systems had "real" controls that could be used a bit
of a distance from the unit, is excusable. Add to that a weird proprietary
RF/power combo (to be bizarrely duplicated again most famously in the Atari
5200) and you have a genuine "what the heck were they thinking?" response.\

 

I will give credit where credit is due though. Games like "Baseball" are
probably as sophisticated as you can get on the platform, so at least in
some ways its performance was "maximized", for whatever that's worth.

 

Interestingly, with one of my units is a typed letter from a mom circa 1982
(it has the exact date on it) requesting more games for the system! Someone
at RCA responded back with a clearance flyer for the few software titles
that were available for it. Imagine actively trying to use the Studio II in
1982?!

Bill Loguidice wrote:
>>
Imagine actively trying to use the Studio II in 1982?!
>>

If you want to get your money's worth then writing to the company is what you have to do.  It's people like this woman that are able to amass large collections of WEIRD and hard to find items.  Heck, what if the letter this mother had gotten back had offered her "Bingo" or something.  Sure, that's not what happened, but I read snippets online or in Retrogamer magazine about people that have items that were thought not to exist because they wrote to the company directly.  Imagine writing to Commavid in 1982 and requesting what games they had and then purchasing Video Life.  That's an extreme example of getting a VERY rare game, but it gets the point across that writing letters used to be one of the best ways to get results.

I was talking to someone YEARS ago (1995?) on the phone (I think that it MIGHT have been Russ Perry Jr.-- Russ was it you?) and this person told me that they knew of a school that STILL used the RCA Studio II as an introduction to single-board computers because the system was so simple.

To bring this back to the Astrocade, I've always thought that the Bally is a great computer for its time.  One of the best, money-wise, in fact.  I've always thought of it, sorta, as more of a single-board computer than as a game console.  The BASIC cartridge allowed users to do very interesting things that no console at the time could have allowed (without additional hardware).  Didn't Brett say recently that he bought the Bally Arcade because it was the best value for the time?  And that, I believe, was at $300.

Adam

If it was first, I would give it much more slack, but besides
the Magnavox Odyssey in 1972 and Atari’s home Pong in 1975, the Fairchild
VES was available in 1976, and got it about as right for a first try at a true
programmable game system as you can get. The fact that the Studio II came in
1977, is black and white, when even color home Pong systems were known
quantities by then, and that it only had keypads on the unit for controls, when
again a variety of systems had “real” controls that could be used a
bit of a distance from the unit, is excusable. Add to that a weird proprietary RF/power
combo (to be bizarrely duplicated again most famously in the Atari 5200) and
you have a genuine “what the heck were they thinking?” response.\

 

I will give credit where credit is due though. Games like “Baseball”
are probably as sophisticated as you can get on the platform, so at least in
some ways its performance was “maximized”, for whatever that’s
worth.

 

Interestingly, with one of my units is a typed letter from a mom
circa 1982 (it has the exact date on it) requesting more games for the system!
Someone at RCA responded back with a clearance flyer for the few software
titles that were available for it. Imagine actively trying to use the Studio II
in 1982?!

I added an ad called, "Astrocade... the home video game that's a computer too!" to the BallyAlley.com flyer section.  This is where I'll be putting one-page color ads from now one.  Besides, I've seen this as an actual flyer before (I thought it was online already, but I can't find it!).

This simple full-page ad, from the October 1982 issue of "Boy's Life," is very simple.  This is what is says:

1) Three Built-in Games
2) Built-in Calculator
3) Octave Music Synthesizer
4) 256 Color Variations
5) Four-Player Capability
6) BASIC Program.

Not ONCE does it say it can play MORE games (it even says, "the home video GAME," nor does this ad have any screenshots.  If I saw this ad, and I knew nothing about the Astrocade already, then I would think that it was a dedicated console without the ability to play cartridges.

When Paul originally scanned this ad, he said, "I have to say, if I had a full page ad, I'd have tried to do a little more with it.  There aren't even any screenshots."  I agree!

I found this old post by Tempest at http://www.atariage.com/forums/topic/71151-videobrain-anyone-have-info/ while searching for information on rumored titles. As promised! I originally wrote this up for inclusion in a guide that never happened, hence the odd formating.

Tempest



VIDEOBRAIN

Ask any of your fellow gamers what they think of the VideoBrain and your likely to get a bunch of blank stares in return. The VideoBrain was an obscure and ultimately short-lived system, yet it holds a special place in computer history as the first cartridge based "computer system" (not video game system).

When it was released in 1977, the VideoBrain came with a sculptured 36 key keyboard (with 71 distinguishable input symbols), 1K of RAM, 4K of ROM, two joysticks and sold for $300. Built into the system where four programs: text editor, clock, alarm, and color bar generator. New programs could be loaded into the system via cartridges which sold from $20 to $40 each. The VideoBrain could be connected to a printer, cassette player, or a modem through special expansion modules. While it may not sound like much now, this was very impressive for 1977.

The VideoBrain library consists mostly of productivity and educational software, with few simulation strategy games mixed in. Most cartridges make liberal use of the keyboard even when it probably wasn't necessary. This was not by accident. The keyboard was one of the main features that separated the VideoBrain from pure video game consoles like the Atari 2600 and was one of its main selling points.


Unfortunately a number of problems plagued the VideoBrain from the start and it was never able to gain a sufficient market share. While most families own at least one computer today, back in 1977 they weren't well understood by the general public. Not helping win people over was the VideoBrain's confusing and non-user friendly keyboard which was poorly designed and makes even simple typing difficult. Another key to the VideoBrain's downfall was that it did not support the popular programming language BASIC. Instead users had to settle for APL/S, an obscure and quirky programming language used mainly by mathematicians. The VideoBrain also had trouble finding a target audience with it's poorly designed program library. Most of the available programs were either productivity or educational in nature with only a smattering of action titles. But what may have been the death nail in the VideoBrain's coffin was lack of advertising and availability. While game systems such as the Atari 2600 were sold in toy and department stores, the VideoBrian was mostly sold directly through the company (via mail order) or in specialty electronics stores.

While the VideoBrain may have been revolutionary for its time, its poorly planned and executed launch doomed the system to an early grave. It wouldn't be until two years later with the arrival of Atari's 400 and 800 computer systems that the public warmed up to the idea of a cartridge based computer system. Even if the VideoBrain had lasted awhile longer it's doubtful that it could have competed against the more powerful and advanced Atari 8-bit computer line.

Blackjack

Catalog Entry: "One or two players try to beat the dealer in a real Nevada style game. Uses 1  2 joysticks."
©1977. EN05

Programmed by Dr. Arthur Samuel
©1977. EN04


Demonstration

While no actual Demonstration cartridge has been found, a cartridge sleeve for it has recently turned up. The cartridge sleeve was actually recycled for use with the Timeshare cartridge, with a sticker placed over the old name.

©1977. ST01


Financier, The

This title was renamed "Money Minder" and re-released with a new part number. Other than the name change, the programs are identical.

Catalog Entry: "A fully prompting program for personal financial use and general household calculations with color graphics display."

©1978. VB-81

Catalog Entry: "A total of 384 action-packed games for Ancient Gladiators, Modern Gladiators, and Future Gladiators. Uses 1  2 joysticks."

Catalog Entry: "Uses exciting graphics and sounds to teach everyone the essentials of economics and business management. A must for young tycoons."

©1978. ED06

Also released as "The Financier", but the name was changed to "Money Minder" a short time later. While new labels were printed up for the cartridges, a large sticker was placed over the old name on the cartridge sleeves. This package was geared towards families, and contained a mix of educational and productivity software. It contained the VideoBrain console, Financier, Math Tutor, Music Teacher 1, Wordwise 1, and Checkers. Originally retailed for $600.

Catalog Entry: "Gives a family a balanced mix of capabilities in the areas of Home Management, Education, and Entertainment. System 300 (The Manager)

This package was designed for home productivity. It contained the VideoBrain console, Financier, Money Minder, and Expander 1. Originally retailed for $700.

This was the top of the line VideoBrain package, specially designed for users who needed to log into timeshare mainframe systems. It contained the VideoBrain console, Money Manager, Financier, Timeshare, Expander 1, and Expander 2. Originally retailed for $1100.

Catalog Entry: "Provides the ultimate system for those who need to use the resources of larger computers at home. Technical Specs.

VideoBrain Specifications
CPU: F-8 Microprocessor 8-bit
Memory: 1K Byte RAM/4K Byte ROM
Inputs: 36 key keyboard (with 71 distinguishable input symbols), 2 X/Y joysticks (capability of up to 4 X/Y analog controls) with hit buttons; cartridge programs (up to 12K bytes of memory each)

>
> When it was released in 1977, the VideoBrain came with a sculptured 36 key keyboard (with 71 distinguishable input symbols), 1K of RAM, 4K of ROM, two joysticks and sold for $300. > VIDEOBRAIN
> 
> Ask any of your fellow gamers what they think of the VideoBrain and your
likely to get a bunch of blank stares in return. The VideoBrain was an
obscure and ultimately short-lived system, yet it holds a special place in
computer history as the first cartridge based "computer system" (not video
game system).
> 
> When it was released in 1977, the VideoBrain came with a sculptured 36 key
keyboard (with 71 distinguishable input symbols), 1K of RAM, 4K of ROM, two
joysticks and sold for $300. Built into the system where four programs: text
editor, clock, alarm, and color bar generator. New programs could be loaded
into the system via cartridges which sold from $20 to $40 each. The
VideoBrain could be connected to a printer, cassette player, or a modem
through special expansion modules. While it may not sound like much now,
this was very impressive for 1977.
> 
> The VideoBrain library consists mostly of productivity and educational
software, with few simulation strategy games mixed in. Most cartridges make
liberal use of the keyboard even when it probably wasn't necessary. This was
not by accident. The keyboard was one of the main features that separated
the VideoBrain from pure video game consoles like the Atari 2600 and was one
of its main selling points.
> 
> 
> Unfortunately a number of problems plagued the VideoBrain from the start
and it was never able to gain a sufficient market share. While most families
own at least one computer today, back in 1977 they weren't well understood
by the general public. Not helping win people over was the VideoBrain's
confusing and non-user friendly keyboard which was poorly designed and makes
even simple typing difficult. Another key to the VideoBrain's downfall was
that it did not support the popular programming language BASIC. Instead
users had to settle for APL/S, an obscure and quirky programming language
used mainly by mathematicians. The VideoBrain also had trouble finding a
target audience with it's poorly designed program library. Most of the
available programs were either productivity or educational in nature with
only a smattering of action titles. But what may have been the death nail in
the VideoBrain's coffin was lack of advertising and availability. While game
systems such as the Atari 2600 were sold in toy and department stores, the
VideoBrian was mostly sold directly through the company (via mail order) or
in specialty electronics stores.
> 
> While the VideoBrain may have been revolutionary for its time, its poorly
planned and executed launch doomed the system to an early grave. It wouldn't
be until two years later with the arrival of Atari's 400 and 800 computer
systems that the public warmed up to the idea of a cartridge based computer
system. Even if the VideoBrain had lasted awhile longer it's doubtful that
it could have competed against the more powerful and advanced Atari 8-bit
computer line.

It's a funny coincidence that I have just added the "Astrocade Owner's" ad to the Bally Alley website.  As it happens, today, on another Yahoo group, Bill and I have posted back and forth about the subject of orphaned computers continuing to be used by their users after the parent company no longer supports the product.  We were specifically talking about the VideoBrain, because it got no support like the Astrocade (and many other systems) received.

Technically this ad was run while Astrocade, Inc. was still in business.  The Astrocade was still being sold and supported.  The support though, was dismal.  There were very few new cartridges.  Most of what Astrocade did was to reissue old cartridges again and make promises that it couldn't keep.  Sure, Astrocade, Inc. DID release a few new games, but it was hardly a trickle.  It was the small companies, many of these usually just one or two people, that tried to take up some of the slack.  These were companies that hardly sold any product, but were committed to supporting Astrocade users.

Usually small companies like this ran small ads in the newsletters like the Arcadian and Cursor.  This half-page ad published in "Electronic Games" is quite different.  It shows what a few people can do when they pool their resources.  Getting an ad into this magazine, as I already said, was expensive, but look what it gave reader's of the magazine access to.  Suddenly, someone that had NO idea that other companies sold software (and hardware!) for the Astrocade were suddenly exposed to a whole new world.  Just look at some of what they saw:

1) Arcadian Newsletter - The Arcadian probably did more for the Bally Arcade and Astrocade than any software or hardware company.  This was the Astrocade owner's connection to the world beyond Montgomery Ward.  Through this resource, Astrocade users could keep in touch with one another.  This contact was the Internet of its day.  This newsletter single-handily created a place for every other advertiser to exist.

2) Astrocade Sourcebook - From here, you could buy just about ANY software for the Astrocade.  In addition, you could get many years of the Arcadian's programs on tape without needing to type them in.  The Sourcebook was also full of advertisements by third-party companies.

3) Bit Fiddlers, The - This company sold the Machine Language Manager cartridge.  It required no extra hardware.  With it, a user could suddenly program in machine language without the VERY cumbersome method required by BASIC.  I still am surprised that this cartridge exists for the Astrocade.  It's a great product with a great manual.

4) George Moses Co. - Some great music for the Astrocade.  While this wasn't unique for computers, most people thought (and continue to think) of the Astrocade as a game console.  Programs like this proved that it was really a computer.

5) Perkins Engineering - The Blue Ram expansion.  With this hardware and RAM upgrade, you could make the Astrocade into a "real" computer.  Actual released products for this were a keyboard, serial adapter (for modem), parallel adapter (for printer), as well as a wonderful, powerful BASIC and a great utility program.  With this hardware, you could have a full-featured computer.

6) R&L Enterprises - The biggest hardware upgrade was available from this company.  This was the 64K RAM board, an amazing piece of hardware.  I only know of ONE of these in existence.

7) Software Companies - Was tape software of the quality of cartridges?  No.  Could it be as fun?  Certainly.  The Bally Alley website has many hundreds of games for the Astrocade that would not exist if it were not for the work of many "bedroom" coders and Jay (AKA Jamie) Fenton (the author of Bally and Astro BASIC).  As Jamie Fenton explained to me in 2001, the Astrocade community sprung up around BASIC.  No one expected it.  Jamie compared the community of BASIC users to the Linux community: people were out to help one another and share the word that what they used was GREAT.  The people who created these programs and games on tape did it out of passion for what they did, not for profit.

8) Spectre Systems - Ah, third-party cartridges.  Unless you saw this ad, or were a subscriber to one of the newsletters, then you simply had NO idea that ICBM Attack existed.

9) Viper System - Alternative Engineering - The Viper 1 is a fantastic upgrade for the Astrocade.  It features 16K RAM and a good basic.

As Bill said about the VideoBrain, for a community to form around a computer (or console), you need a programming language.  The Astrocade had BASIC, and because of it a community sprung up and grew.  This gave the Astrocade plenty of support-- you just had to look in the right places.

Adam

I called ballsy. I would imagine one is from mid-1977 and other late 1977,

and Commodore PET, so it's fascinating that Bally would so quickly target
them and other computers as competition like that. Based on those two sales
flyers/brochures, it seems the Astrocade was originally intended as the
lowest cost possible practical personal computer rather than a videogame
console, which explains a lot of what happened in terms of the platform's
future. They obviously scaled back those ambitions quickly for whatever
reason, and it's probably related to costs and feasibility of including
certain elements. They probably scaled back dramatically and decided, "hey,
we'll add it later", which hindsight proved was not to be. Heck, if they
even included the intended serial port among the list of whiz bang features,

8104:
When the 1200 baud rate was popular, bask in the 70's, they were saying that when they had problems receiving or sending they blamed it on the phone system which really wasn't geared for anything but voice, and that wasn't always good. The transfer points were all relay contacts, and there was no such thing as "twisted-pair" wiring. There was a lot of line loss because it was all over land wires. So when 2400 baud came out, they were thought to be stretching the limit. then eventually came the short-lived 48K rate.
Finally the end of the common rates was reached when 56K baud became popular. This forced the phone companies to upgrade their systems to solid state to keep the public from tearing their heads off. That stayed the same for so long that people were wondering if there was going to be any way to increase the speed. The PBX that businesses were using was so much faster and then poeple went home to their "Putt-Putt" computers
Next step was DSL, but ONLY if you were lucky enough to be close enough to a switching station. All of this coupled with the fact that there were different phone companies (GTE, Bell, and General, as well as small independents) whose equipment was different. So you can see how this made a mess of everything that was going on at the time.

One other tid-bit that Mike told me was that Music Maker and AstroBASIC did not output the same to the tape.  For whatever reason, a '1' sent to tape from Music Maker would be a '0' sent to tape from AstroBASIC.  And, of course, the opposite also holds true.  A '0' sent to tape from Music Maker would be a '1' sent to tape from
AstroBASIC.  I wonder why they would make the software opposite like that?  We've never archived any Music Maker music before, but if we did I wonder if Astrobin would BallyWAV would still work?  Probably not.  The archiving software doesn't care what a '1' or a '0' means, but it does need the leading tone and ending tone, which might not be the same between the two pieces of software.

Toby and Ken, you both have this cartridge (does anybody else?), have either of you ever been able to save from your Music Maker cartridge?  Have you ever tried?

From: Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com>

Subject: [ballyalley] Comments on "Astrocade Owners!" Ad



It's a funny coincidence that I have just added the "Astrocade Owner's" ad to the Bally Alley website.  As it happens, today, on another Yahoo group, Bill and I have posted back and forth about the subject of orphaned computers continuing to be used by their users after the parent company no longer supports the product.  We were specifically talking about the VideoBrain, because it got no support like the Astrocade (and many other systems) received.

Technically this ad was run while Astrocade, Inc. was still in business.  The Astrocade was still being sold and supported.  The support though, was dismal.  There were very few new cartridges.  Most of what Astrocade did was to reissue old cartridges again and make promises that it couldn't keep.  Sure, Astrocade, Inc. DID release a few new games, but it was hardly a trickle.  It was the small companies, many of these usually just one or two people, that tried to take up some of the slack.  These were companies that hardly sold any product, but were committed to supporting Astrocade users.

Usually small companies like this ran small ads in the newsletters like the Arcadian and Cursor.  This half-page ad published in "Electronic Games" is quite different.  It shows what a few people can do when they pool their resources.  Getting an ad into this magazine, as I already said, was expensive, but look what it gave reader's of the magazine access to.  Suddenly, someone that had NO idea that other companies sold software (and hardware!) for the Astrocade were suddenly exposed to a whole new world.  Just look at some of what they saw:

1) Arcadian Newsletter - The Arcadian probably did more for the Bally Arcade and Astrocade than any software or hardware company.  This was the Astrocade owner's connection to the world beyond Montgomery Ward.  Through this resource, Astrocade users could keep in touch with one another.  This contact was the Internet of its day.  This newsletter single-handily created a place for every other advertiser to exist.

2) Astrocade Sourcebook - From here, you could buy just about ANY software for the Astrocade.  In addition, you could get many years of the Arcadian's programs on tape without needing to type them in.  The Sourcebook was also full of advertisements by third-party companies.

3) Bit Fiddlers, The - This company sold the Machine Language Manager cartridge.  It required no extra hardware.  With it, a user could suddenly program in machine language without the VERY cumbersome method required by BASIC.  I still am surprised that this cartridge exists for the Astrocade.  It's a great product with a great manual.

4) George Moses Co. - Some great music for the Astrocade.  While this wasn't unique for computers, most people thought (and continue to think) of the Astrocade as a game console.  Programs like this proved that it was really a computer.

5) Perkins Engineering - The Blue Ram expansion.  With this hardware and RAM upgrade, you could make the Astrocade into a "real" computer.  Actual released products for this were a keyboard, serial adapter (for modem), parallel adapter (for printer), as well as a wonderful, powerful BASIC and a great utility program.  With this hardware, you could have a full-featured computer.

6) R&L Enterprises - The biggest hardware upgrade was available from this company.  This was the 64K RAM board, an amazing piece of hardware.  I only know of ONE of these in existence.

7) Software Companies - Was tape software of the quality of cartridges?  No.  Could it be as fun?  Certainly.  The Bally Alley website has many hundreds of games for the Astrocade that would not exist if it were not for the work of many "bedroom" coders and Jay (AKA Jamie) Fenton (the author of Bally and Astro BASIC).  As Jamie Fenton explained to me in 2001, the Astrocade community sprung up around BASIC.  No one expected it.  Jamie compared the community of BASIC users to the Linux community: people were out to help one another and share the word that what they used was GREAT.  The people who created these programs and games on tape did it out of passion for what they did, not for profit.

8) Spectre Systems - Ah, third-party cartridges.  Unless you saw this ad, or were a subscriber to one of the newsletters, then you simply had NO idea that ICBM Attack existed.

9) Viper System - Alternative Engineering - The Viper 1 is a fantastic upgrade for the Astrocade.  It features 16K RAM and a good basic.

As Bill said about the VideoBrain, for a community to form around a computer (or console), you need a programming language.  The Astrocade had BASIC, and because of it a community sprung up and grew.  This gave the Astrocade plenty of support-- you just had to look in the right places.

Adam

8207:
I meant to mention this earlier.  I figured-out a FAST way to get straight pictures from crooked scans using Photoshop.  As long as the scan is at least 200DPI or do then this method works very well.  With lower-quality scans, the method DOES work, but the "fix" may be noticeable.

You'll notice that the tape scans that I've uploaded today are straight.  The cartridge scans that I'll be uploading later (maybe tomorrow) are also straight (not to mention FAR better quality-- and CLEANER too!).

For those that have Photoshop, here is how to straighten a picture (I'm presuming plenty of experience with Photoshop here):

1)  Select the "Measure Tool" (Right-Click on the "Eye Dropper" Tool to choose it).

2)  Draw a line along a crooked edge that you want to now be the horizontal straight line for the picture.

3)  Choose Tools> Rotate Canvas> Arbitrary

4) Normally when you choose "Arbitrary" you put in a number, say 23%.  Now you don't have to do that.  There will be a number already there, usually about 1-2%.  This is the exact number needed to make the picture straight.  Just click okay.

5)  You're picture is now straight.  Trim the edges and you're done.

Note that you can NOT straighten a B&W picture; the picture must be grayscale or color.  Of course, you can always convert a B&W picture to grayscale, straighten it, then convert it back to B&W, but you WILL notice that the picture quality is reduced.

I learned this method when I was making a photo album for my wife.  I wish that someone had taught me this simple trick years ago.  I hope that this helps anyone using Photoshop... you'll find it's extremely useful.

Adam
